HVAC Technician Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

An HVAC technician resume has to prove one thing above all: that you can keep a system running, fix it fast when it stops, and leave a customer ready to call you back. Hiring managers do not hire on a list of tools. They hire on certifications, system range, and a record of installs and repairs finished cleanly with customers who renew.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, the skills hiring sides scan for, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

Quick answer: A HVAC technician resume should open with your EPA 608 certification and trade experience, name the systems and sites you worked on, show maintenance contracts and clean service records, list your licenses and certifications, and prove reliability on real installs — then keep the layout single-column with standard headings so tracking systems parse every section cleanly.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with your EPA 608 certification and trade level — what you are certified to do, and where.
  • Prove reliability with maintenance contracts kept, callbacks avoided, and systems kept running.
  • Name the systems, sites, and scale from the posting.
  • Every bullet pairs a task with a result: what you installed or repaired, where, and what changed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What HVAC Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a service manager or a lead technician and you will not hear "passionate about air conditioning." You will hear:

  • EPA 608 certification and trade level. Universal EPA 608, state license, apprenticeship completed — checked before anything else.
  • System range. Split systems, heat pumps, furnaces, rooftop units, chillers, boilers, ductwork, and controls — name the systems and sites you actually worked on.
  • Maintenance contracts kept. A contract renewed, a system that stayed running, a callback avoided. "Sixty contracts renewed" is a hiring signal; "worked hard" is not.
  • Diagnostics under pressure. Finding a refrigerant leak, a failed compressor, a control fault — and fixing it without tearing a home apart. Fast diagnosis beats fast installation.
  • Safety and refrigerant handling. Refrigerant recovery, electrical safety, combustion safety, and a clean safety record. A resume with no mention of safe handling tells a hiring manager your work is a risk.

If your resume reads like a tool list — all gauges and wrenches, no systems — it will lose to a work record.

HVAC Technician Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a licensed HVAC technician with residential service and light-commercial install experience. It is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

DEREK LAWSON — Licensed HVAC Technician
Denver, CO · (303) 555-0182 · derek.lawson@email.com · EPA 608 Universal · Licensed in CO

SUMMARY
Licensed HVAC technician with 9 years of residential service and light-commercial install work. Led a 4-person crew retrofitting HVAC in a 240-unit apartment complex; cut callbacks from 15% to 5% in one year and kept 60 maintenance contracts renewing. Heat pumps, split systems, furnaces, rooftop units; EPA 608 Universal, NATE, OSHA 30.

CERTIFICATIONS
EPA 608 Universal · NATE Heat Pump Certification · OSHA 30-Hour Construction · Refrigerant Handling · CPR / First Aid

SKILLS
Heat pump installation & repair · Split system installation · Furnace repair & replacement · Rooftop unit service · Chiller maintenance · Boiler service · Ductwork design & install · Refrigerant leak detection · Thermostat & controls · Preventive maintenance · Load calculation · Crew leadership · Code compliance

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

HVAC Technician — Mile High Climate, Denver, CO | 2021–Present - Led a 4-person crew retrofitting HVAC in a 240-unit apartment complex, finishing 3 weeks ahead of schedule with zero failed inspections - Cut callbacks from 15% to 5% with a post-install checklist and a same-day follow-up call routine, saving 80 crew-hours in one year - Serviced 60 maintenance contracts a year, keeping renewals high with same-day response on every emergency call - Traced a recurring refrigerant leak two earlier callouts had missed, using electronic detection to find the break and repair it the same day - Train 3 apprentices; two of my apprentices passed their EPA 608 exams on the first attempt

HVAC Service Technician — Front Range Heating & Air, Denver, CO | 2018–2021 - Ran 20 service calls a week across the city, from furnace repairs to full system replacements, keeping every job inside its window - Installed heat pumps and split systems across 12 restaurant fit-outs, including rooftop units and ventilation - Read load calculations and marked up duct layouts, catching 5 airflow clashes before they reached the site - Covered the lead technician's holidays, running small commercial jobs end to end with no callbacks

HVAC Apprentice — Rocky Mountain Mechanical, Denver, CO | 2016–2018 - Worked the install crew on 70-unit residential builds, learning the pace of a real construction schedule - Set condensers, ran line sets, and brazed joints on commercial fit-outs, with a zero-missed-material record in the final year - Earned promotion to technician after completing the apprenticeship and passing the EPA 608 exam

EDUCATION
HVAC Apprenticeship — Associated Builders and Contractors, Denver, CO, 2016–2020 High School Diploma — East High School, Denver, CO, 2016

Why it works: the summary leads with the two things HVAC hiring managers check first — EPA 608 certification and systems kept running (240 units, callbacks 15% to 5%, 60 contracts) — then names the systems. Every bullet pairs a task with a result: faster install, fewer callbacks.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: certification, scope, service record

"EPA 608 Universal," "240-unit apartment complex," "callbacks from 15% to 5%," "60 maintenance contracts" — four facts that place you in thirty seconds. Lead with certification and a result, not training.

Experience: jobs with outcomes, not duties

"Installed HVAC in a commercial building" is a duty; "cut callbacks from 15% to 5% while holding the install schedule" is proof. Units retrofitted, contracts kept, callback rates, and crew size are the metrics that matter.

Systems and sites: proof you can work the trade

Your range is the closest thing to proof an HVAC technician gets. Name the systems you actually installed — heat pumps, split systems, furnaces, rooftop units — and the sites behind them. One vague claim costs more than a missing skill — list only work you could do tomorrow.

Skills: mirror the posting, honestly

List the systems and tools you have actually worked with, in the posting's own words — "refrigerant leak detection" versus "repair work" matters to filters, as does "preventive maintenance" versus "service calls." Depth in one part of the trade beats a long list.

HVAC Technician Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "heat pump installation" vs "HVAC work" matters to filters:

  • Systems: heat pump installation, split system installation, furnace repair, rooftop unit service, chiller maintenance, boiler service, ductwork design
  • Work types: residential service calls, light-commercial installs, remodels, restaurant fit-outs, maintenance contracts, emergency repair
  • Safety & handling: EPA 608, refrigerant recovery, electrical safety, combustion safety, OSHA 30, inspection readiness, permit coordination
  • Tools & reading: load calculation, duct layout reading, thermostat & controls, leak detection, brazing, crew leadership

HVAC companies screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. 5 Mistakes That Cost HVAC Technicians Interviews

  1. A tool list, not a work record. A long list of tools with no systems, contracts, or installs reads as a hobbyist. Add numbers that show you finished it.
  2. Hiding the EPA 608 certification. If your certification and license level are buried at the bottom, a hiring manager may never reach them. Put certification in the summary and header.
  3. Duties without results. "Installed HVAC in homes" could describe anyone on a crew. Add the result — fewer callbacks, faster install, a crew trained — to every bullet.
  4. Vague system claims. List what you installed, job after job.
  5. Ignoring safety and refrigerant handling. A resume with no mention of refrigerant recovery, electrical safety, or a clean safety record tells a hiring manager your work is a risk. Put safety up front.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do HVAC technicians need EPA 608 certification to work?

Yes, in almost every case. Anyone who handles refrigerants must hold EPA 608 certification under federal rules, and most employers ask for it before anything else. Universal certification covers all equipment types, so list it at the top of your resume with your state license.

What experience should a new HVAC technician put on a resume?

Lead with jobs and scope. An apprenticeship on a busy build, a system retrofit, or a furnace replacement all count. Name what you installed, how many units, and what changed — the same pattern as a senior bullet.

How do I show maintenance contracts and reliability on an HVAC resume?

Name the record: contracts kept, callbacks avoided, and systems kept running — contracts renewed, emergency calls answered same day, installs finished on schedule. "60 contracts renewed with same-day emergency response" tells a manager more than any adjective.

Should an HVAC technician resume include photos of my work?

No — keep the resume itself text-only so tracking systems can parse it, and put job photos in a separate portfolio or social profile linked from the header. A photo inside the resume file is usually stripped or misread by the parser.

How long should an HVAC technician resume be?

One page for most HVAC technicians, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across different work — residential service, commercial installs, maintenance contracts — and even then keep your best numbers on page one.

Do I need to list every job I have ever held as an HVAC technician?

No. List the jobs that show your trade range and your most recent work — usually the last 10 to 15 years, including your apprenticeship if it is your foundation. Older short roles can be dropped, but keep the timeline honest: a gap with no explanation raises more questions than a short role ever will.
